31. After considering the above submissions and analysing the evidence of the said PWs we find that PW 13 though a child witness of tender age gave intelligent answers to the questions put to him and he is a very natural and truthful witness and we have no hesitation in relying on his evidence. We also find that PW 12, who is a student of Class VII, though a minor can not be termed as a child witness and he is also another direct witness like PW 13 of the two accused appellant hiring rickshaw van of their brother Khalil and taking away Khalil by the accused with the van who did not return home and subsequently dead body of Khalil being found and PW 12 identifying the dead body in the PS. Evidence of these two witnesses could not be shaken in cross-examination. The learned trial Judge who had the ad-vantage of seeing their demeanour in the dock also found them natural witnesses like the other witnesses and relied on their evidence. Facts of the case of Hamida Begum Vs. the State reported in PLD 1978 SC (Al & K) 102 relied on by the learned Advocate of the appellants is not binding on us and has no relevancy in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. Rather we are fortified in our view by the decision in the case of State Vs. Badiuzzaman reported in 25 DLR Dhaka 41 wherein it has been held that person who can understand questions and can give rational answers to them is a competent witness. In that case testimony of a boy of 13 years was relied on. 

 40. There is no mandatory provision of law that the accused are to be given 3 hours time for reflection (vide the case of Ratan Kha Vs. The State 40 DLR 186). On consideration of the evidence of PW 27 and the two confessional statements Ext. 3 & 4 we are satisfied that one of the accused got at least 3 hours time for reflection and the other accused got 2 hours time for reflection. The Magistrate did not notice any injury marks on the body of the accused persons and no such complaint appears to have been made to the Magistrate by the accused. The accused were sent to jail custody after their confessional statements were recorded by the Magistrate. Defence failed to produce any paper showing that accused Abul Kashem was admitted in the Jail Hospital as a result of beating by the police. In the record there is jail ticket of the prisoner Abbasuddin in which there is an entry that he was admitted in the jail hospital on 29.4.86 and he was released from the jail hospital subsequently but the portion of that ticket containing the date of release from the hospital being torn the date of release could not be ascertained. We are satisfied that the two confessional statements of accused Abbasuddin and Abul Kashem recorded on the next day of their arrest are voluntary. 

 43. In the case of State Vs. Lalu Mia and another reported in 39 DLR (AD) 117=1987 BLD (AD) 212 one member Ashraf Ali was alleged to have been murdered by the said Lalu and his cousin and co-accused Kabiruddin. In that case there was no eye-witness of the murderer The two accused were seen to have accompanied the deceased to Sreemongal town in the evening and the deceased was last seen in Sreemongal town with the two accused persons and as the deceased did not return home his brother searched for the deceased and on the next morning the beheaded body and also the severed head of the deceased were recovered from beneath the water hyacinth of the tank. In that case all the circumstances before and after the murder were proved by independent evidence implicating the two accused for the murder though none witnessed the murder of deceased Ashraf Ali. In that case the motive of murder was shown to be deprivation of the accused Lalu by the deceased from the management of the property of one Afsa Khatun who was owner of vast properties and who married the deceased 3 days before the occurrence. In that case both the accused persons made confessional statements. One of the accused Kabiruddin made the confessional statement within 24 hours of his arrest and the other accused Lalu made the confessional statement after several days of his arrest. In that case the question about admissibility and extent of reliance to be placed on the confessional statement of co-accused Kabiruddin being partly inculpatory and party exculpatory came for consideration. His Lordship Mr. Justice BH Chowdhury, as his Lordship then was, delivering the majority judgment of the court after considering the several decisions on the question held that the inculpatory part of the confessional statement of accused Kabir admitting concealing the severed head of the deceased can be relied on for convicting him for concealing the evidence of murder as exculpatory part of his confessional statement that he did not participate in the murder of the deceased though he admitted to be present there at the time of murder was improbable and false and his confessional statement can also be used for lending assurance under section 30 of the Evidence Act against the co-accused Lalu. The learned Judge also held that the confessional statement of accused Lalu was free and voluntary and the same could also be relied upon. His Lordship Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed, as his Lordship then was, while delivering a separate judgement concurring with the majority judgment in that case held that the confessional statement of accused Lalu was not free and voluntary and he could not be convicted relying upon the said confessional statement. But his Lordships further held that the confessional statement of accused Kabir is voluntary though the same is partly exculpatory and partly inculpatory; the exculpatory part of his statement that he happened to be present at the scene of crime just by coincidence is false being contrary to reason and human conduct and as such liable to be rejected as utter falsehood and inculpatory part of his confessional statement that he concealed the severed head of the deceased can be relied on for convicting him for concealing the dead body and can be considered against the other accused Lalu under section 30 of the Evidence Act as both of them were tried together for committing the same offence.
